extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy (Aristotle / ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing Aristotle's criteria and distinctions about self-control (enkrateia), its defects, the nature and value of pleasure and pain, and the kinds and conditions of friendship from Nicomachean Ethics (Books VII–VIII).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-Control (Enkrateia)
rubrics_metrics.description: The character who does not yield to bodily pleasures or pains contrary to Right Reason; actual mastery (not merely continued resistance) in abiding by one's conclusions and moral choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-Control is choice-worthy and distinct from Endurance; the self-controlled person feels contrary pleasures but does not yield to them. He abides by true conclusions and moral choice rather than by impulse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfect Self-Control (Akrasia)
rubrics_metrics.description: A state where a person follows bodily pleasures in excess and in defiance of Right Reason, without acting on any deliberate conviction; passion prevents acting in accordance with Right Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comes in two forms: Precipitancy (no prior resolutions; swept away by sudden temptation) and Weakness (has made resolutions but does not abide by them because of passion). Such persons are often remorseful and potentially curable; they are not confirmed viciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utter Absence of Self-Control (Confirmed Vice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The character who acts upon a conviction grounded in natural inclination to follow pleasures (i.e., believes limitless pursuit of pleasure is proper), is incurable and lacks remorse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinct from akrasia: this person is formed by vice and preserves the moral principle in a corrupt form; worse morally because he acts on settled conviction rather than being overcome despite better judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Softness (Malakia) and Luxury
rubrics_metrics.description: A character marked by yielding to avoid ordinary troubles and pains (e.g., letting one’s robe drag to avoid lifting it), a kind of excess in the relaxation/amusement sphere; often mistaken for lack of self-control but distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Softness is especially shown by avoiding ordinary efforts and by excessive pursuit of amusement (an act of resting). It is closer to luxury and differs from utter lack of self-control in cause and expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endurance (Hypomone) vs Mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: Endurance consists in continued resistance to pain or temptation, whereas Self-Control is actual mastery (conquering rather than merely not being conquered).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-Control is more choice-worthy than Endurance because it involves active mastery rather than mere persistence; the two are different virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precipitancy and Weakness (subtypes of akrasia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Precipitancy: failure due to never forming resolutions and being swept by passion (more common in sharp/melancholy temperaments). Weakness: having resolutions but failing to keep them because of passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precipitants are liable to act without deliberation; the weak are like those overcome by sleep or wine. Precipitancy often arises from swiftness or violence of passions; weakness involves remorse and is more amenable to cure by habituation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remorse as diagnostic of akrasia
rubrics_metrics.description: Imperfect Self-Control is typically accompanied by remorse, whereas utter absence of self-control (confirmed vice) is not given to remorse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of remorse indicates the agent still retains the moral principle and is thus potentially curable; absence suggests settled depravity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral assessment must consider motive and conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: An action done without impulse of desire or with a very slight impulse is often judged worse than the same action done under a strong desire; moral blame depends on whether action stemmed from conviction or was compelled by passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging character, consider whether the agent acted from settled belief (worse) or under overwhelming passion despite better judgment (less culpable). Examples: striking when not angry versus in wrath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and ethical status of Pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Three views exist: (1) no pleasure is good (distinct from good), (2) some pleasures are good but most are bad, (3) every pleasure is good but Pleasure is not the Chief Good. Aristotle argues pleasures can be good per se in some senses and distinguishes bodily pleasures from higher pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasures may be: active workings of a natural state (choice-worthy), mere processes (remedial), bodily (often accompanied by desire and liable to excess), or intellectual (higher, not impediments to thought). The ethical value of a pleasure depends on its kind, relation to nature, and whether it is excessive or remedial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for deeming pleasures 'base' or 'hurtful'
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodily pleasures accompanied by desire and pain, or those pursued to excess (producing disease), are base and blameworthy; some pleasures are remedial (pleasant because they cure a deficiency) and not intrinsically good per se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate pleasures that perfect an active state (good) from violent or remedial pleasures that are pursued only to relieve pain; the latter are often the object of the low/bad man's pursuit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure as active working vs process
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is not simply a sensible process toward completion but can be an unimpeded active working of a natural state (e.g., intellectual activity), and such pleasures can be ends in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate process and active working; some pleasures (especially intellectual) are immediate activities and can be central to the happy life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of Pleasure and Pain in Happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness (eudaimonia) involves unimpeded active working; pleasure accompanies and completes this life. Bodily goods and external fortune are additions required so active working is not fettered; but pleasure alone is not identical with happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While higher pleasures may be integral to the happy life, external goods and absence of impediments matter; denying pleasure entirely undermines the intelligibility of happiness because the happy life's activities can be pleasant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship: necessary conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship requires mutual kindly feelings (wishing good for the other) that are reciprocated and mutually known; mere kindly disposition without mutual knowledge is 'kindliness' not full friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To count as friendship there must be (1) reciprocated kindly feelings, (2) wish for the other’s good, and (3) mutual awareness of those feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects/motives of Friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three objects/motives of friendship: (a) the good, (b) the pleasurable, and (c) the useful. Friendships correspond to these motives and differ in nature and durability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friendship for the good aims at another’s real good (more lasting); friendship for pleasure or utility is instrumental and liable to dissolution when pleasure or utility ceases. Determine whether the friend is loved for who he is (good) or for what he provides (pleasure/use).

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship as relative to individual's perception of good
rubrics_metrics.description: People feel friendship toward what appears to be good for them; abstractly the object is the real good, but in practice each loves what seems good to himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the distinction between objective goods and what individuals take to be good for themselves; friendship may be grounded in perceived benefit rather than absolute goodness, which affects stability and moral worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics and consequences of different friendship types
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships of utility and pleasure are results-based and often lack intimate intercourse; they dissolve when the underlying advantage or pleasure ceases. Friendships grounded in the good are more stable and intimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Older people more often form utility friendships; those seeking pleasure form pleasure friendships. True friendships (for good) involve desire for the other's sake and persistent mutual concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and political value of Friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship appears implanted by Nature, necessary for life, aids various ages, binds social communities, and is a principal aim of legislators (even more than Justice) because it fosters unanimity and reduces faction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In political or social evaluation, value friendship highly as a foundation of community and practical life; legislators should cultivate it to promote social cohesion.
